records.title: Who Created Python?

quick_facts.label: Why it was created
quick_facts.value: To make programming easier to read, write, and understand

records.definition: Python was created by **Guido van Rossum**, a Dutch programmer.
records.explanation: Guido van Rossum began designing Python in December 1989 while working at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica) in Amsterdam, Netherlands. He wanted a language that was easy to read, enjoyable to use, and better than the ABC language he had worked on previously. The first public release appeared on February 20, 1991.
records.fun_fact: Python is named after the British comedy series 'Monty Python's Flying Circus', not the snake!
records.image_caption: Guido van Rossum — Creator of Python

records.title: When Was Python First Released?
records.definition: Python was **first publicly released on February 20, 1991** as version 0.9.0.
records.explanation: Guido van Rossum started developing Python in December 1989. The first public release was version 0.9.0 on February 20, 1991 — it already included functions, exception handling, and core data types. Python 1.0 arrived in 1994, Python 2.0 in 2000, and the major Python 3.0 in December 2008. Python 2 officially reached end-of-life in 2020.
records.fun_fact: Python 0.9.0 already had many features considered modern even today — classes, functions, and exception handling were all there from the start.

records.title: Where Was Python Created?
records.definition: Python was created at **CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica)** in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.
records.explanation: CWI is a national research institute for mathematics and computer science in the Netherlands. Guido van Rossum was working there when he began developing Python in December 1989 as a side project during the holiday season. The institute provided the environment and resources that made Python possible.
records.fun_fact: Guido van Rossum started Python as a hobby project to keep himself busy during the Christmas break of 1989!

quick_facts.label: Key design principle

records.definition: Python was created to make programming **easier to read, write, and understand** — a successor to the ABC language with better extensibility.
records.explanation: Guido van Rossum was frustrated with ABC's limitations — it had good ideas but couldn't be extended easily. He wanted a language that: kept ABC's readability, allowed system calls (which ABC couldn't do), supported exception handling, and could be extended. Python's guiding philosophy became 'There should be one obvious way to do it', captured in 'The Zen of Python'.
records.fun_fact: Python was born from frustration — Guido wanted to fix what he loved about ABC while adding what it was missing.

records.title: Python Version History and Milestones

quick_facts.value: Python 1.0 — added lambda, map, filter, reduce

records.definition: Python has evolved through major versions: 0.9 (1991), 1.0 (1994), 2.0 (2000), and 3.0 (2008). Python 3 is the current and only supported version.
records.explanation:
Key milestones:
- 1991: Python 0.9.0 — classes, functions, exception handling
- 1994: Python 1.0 — functional tools added
- 2000: Python 2.0 — list comprehensions, Unicode support
- 2008: Python 3.0 — fixed design flaws, broke backward compatibility
- 2020: Python 2 officially discontinued

The Python 2 to 3 transition was the biggest change in Python's history. Code written for Python 2 does not automatically run on Python 3.
records.fun_fact: The Python 2-to-3 transition took over 10 years because so many organisations depended on Python 2 code.

records.title: What Is Python?
keywords: may i know what is python
records.definition: Python is a **high-level, general-purpose, interpreted programming language** known for its clean, readable syntax and large ecosystem of libraries.
records.explanation:
Python lets you write programs that are easy to read and understand. Unlike languages like C or Java, Python code looks almost like plain English — you use indentation to define code blocks instead of curly braces. Python runs programs line by line through an interpreter, which makes development fast and interactive.

Python is used for web development, data science, artificial intelligence, automation, scientific computing, and much more.
records.fun_fact: Python consistently ranks as one of the top 3 most popular programming languages worldwide.
records.image_caption: Guido van Rossum — Creator of Python

records.title: What Is Python Used For?
records.definition: Python is widely used in **web development, data science, artificial intelligence, automation, and scientific computing**.
records.explanation:
Python's versatility makes it popular across many fields:
- Web: Django and Flask power websites
- Data: pandas and NumPy for analysis
- AI/ML: TensorFlow and scikit-learn for models
- Automation: scripts to automate repetitive tasks
- Education: often the first language taught because of its readability
- Finance: algorithms and data processing
- Games: Pygame for simple games
records.fun_fact: Instagram, YouTube, Dropbox, and NASA all use Python in their systems.

records.title: Key Characteristics of Python

quick_facts.label: Readable syntax
quick_facts.value: Uses indentation, reads like plain English

quick_facts.label: Dynamically typed
quick_facts.value: No need to declare variable types

records.definition: Python is known for its **readable syntax, dynamic typing, large standard library, and cross-platform compatibility**.
records.explanation:
Core characteristics:
- Readable: code indentation makes structure clear
- Dynamically typed: type(x) is determined at runtime
- Batteries included: math, files, networking all in the standard library
- Cross-platform: same code runs everywhere
- Large ecosystem: hundreds of thousands of third-party packages on PyPI
- Garbage collected: memory is managed automatically
- Interactive: Python REPL for testing code instantly
records.fun_fact: Python's philosophy is summarised in 'The Zen of Python' — type 'import this' in Python to read it.

records.title: Python Programming Paradigms

quick_facts.label: Style
quick_facts.value: Multi-paradigm — use any or all styles

records.definition: Python is a **multi-paradigm language** — it supports procedural, object-oriented, and functional programming styles.
records.explanation:
You can write Python in three main styles:
1. Procedural: write functions and call them in order
2. Object-oriented: organise code into classes and objects
3. Functional: use map(), filter(), lambda, and list comprehensions

Most Python code mixes styles — use whatever fits the problem. This flexibility is one reason Python is used both for quick scripts and large applications.
records.fun_fact: Python's flexibility means a beginner can write procedural code and an expert can use advanced functional patterns — all in the same language.

records.title: How Does Python Run / Execute Code?

quick_facts.label: Process
quick_facts.value: Source code → bytecode → executed by PVM

quick_facts.label: Speed
quick_facts.value: Slower than C/Java but fast enough for most tasks

quick_facts.label: Interactive
quick_facts.value: Can run code line by line in the REPL

records.definition: Python is an **interpreted language** — the Python interpreter reads and executes code line by line without compiling to machine code first.
records.explanation:
How Python actually runs your code:
1. You write source code in a .py file
2. CPython (the standard Python interpreter) reads the file
3. It converts source to bytecode (.pyc files)
4. The Python Virtual Machine (PVM) executes the bytecode

This differs from C which compiles directly to machine code, making C faster but Python faster to develop with. Python also supports an interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) where you can test single lines instantly.
records.fun_fact: CPython is written in C — so Python the language is actually implemented in a compiled language for performance.

records.title: Variables in Python
aliases: how to declare a variable in python
records.definition: A variable in Python is a named label that stores a value. You create a variable by writing its name, the equals sign, and the value. Python figures out the type automatically.
records.explanation:
In Python you do not need to declare a type before using a variable. Simply assign a value:

    name = 'Alice'
    age = 20
    gpa = 3.9
    is_enrolled = True

Python uses dynamic typing, meaning the same variable can hold different types at different times. Variable names must start with a letter or underscore, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive (age and Age are different).

Best practices:
- Use descriptive, lowercase names: student_name, not sn.
- Use snake_case for multi-word names: first_name, not firstName.
- Use ALL_CAPS for constants by convention: MAX_SIZE = 100.

Checking the type: use type(variable) to see what type a variable holds.
common_mistakes: Starting a variable name with a digit (2name is invalid)
Using a reserved keyword as a name (if, for, class)
Confusing = (assignment) with == (comparison)

records.title: Data Types in Python
aliases: what are the data types in python
records.definition: Python has several built-in data types. The most common are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), and bool (True or False).
records.explanation:
Core built-in types:
- int: whole numbers, e.g. 42, -7, 0.
- float: decimal numbers, e.g. 3.14, -0.5.
- str: text enclosed in quotes, e.g. 'hello' or "world".
- bool: True or False (capital T and F).
- NoneType: the special value None meaning 'no value'.

Type conversion (casting):
    int('42')     # 42
    float('3.14') # 3.14
    str(100)      # '100'
    bool(0)       # False

Python is dynamically typed: you do not declare types — Python infers them. Use type(x) to check. Use isinstance(x, int) to test.

Truthy and falsy: 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, None all evaluate as False in a condition. Everything else is True.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert input() result from str before arithmetic
Comparing int and str with == (always False)
Confusing None with False or 0

records.title: Operators in Python
records.definition: Operators are symbols that perform operations on values. Python has arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, and membership operators.
records.explanation:
Arithmetic operators:
    +  addition         5 + 3 = 8
    -  subtraction      5 - 3 = 2
    *  multiplication   5 * 3 = 15
    /  true division    7 / 2 = 3.5   (always float)
    // floor division   7 // 2 = 3    (integer result)
    %  modulo           7 % 2 = 1     (remainder)
    ** exponentiation   2 ** 3 = 8

Comparison operators (return True or False):
    ==  equal to
    !=  not equal to
    <   less than
    >   greater than
    <=  less than or equal
    >=  greater than or equal

Logical operators:
    and  — both conditions must be True
    or   — at least one condition must be True
    not  — inverts a boolean

Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, *=, //=, **=, %=

Membership operators: in, not in (check if a value is in a sequence)

Identity operators: is, is not (check if two variables point to the same object)

Precedence (highest first): ** → unary - → * / // % → + - → comparisons → not → and → or
common_mistakes: Using = instead of == in conditions
Expecting / to give an integer result (use // for that)
Forgetting operator precedence — use parentheses to be explicit

records.title: Conditional Statements in Python
records.definition: A conditional statement runs a block of code only when a condition is True. Python uses if, elif, and else keywords.
common_mistakes: Using = instead of == in the condition
Forgetting the colon (:) after if/elif/else
Wrong indentation causing logic errors

records.title: Loops in Python
records.definition: Loops repeat a block of code. Python has two loop types: for (iterates over a sequence) and while (repeats while a condition is True).
records.explanation:
For loop — iterates over any iterable (list, string, range, etc.):
    for item in [1, 2, 3]:
        print(item)

    for i in range(5):       # 0 1 2 3 4
        print(i)

    for i in range(2, 10, 2):  # 2 4 6 8 — start, stop, step
        print(i)

While loop — repeats as long as condition is True:
    count = 0
    while count < 5:
        print(count)
        count += 1

Loop control:
    break    — exits the loop immediately
    continue — skips the rest of this iteration, goes to next
    pass     — does nothing, used as a placeholder

For-else and while-else: the else block runs only if the loop completed without a break.

Nested loops: a loop inside a loop. The inner loop runs fully for each iteration of the outer loop.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one errors with range (range(5) gives 0–4, not 1–5)
Forgetting to update the while loop condition (causes infinite loop)
Modifying a list while iterating over it
records.source_name: Python Documentation — More Control Flow Tools

records.title: Functions in Python
aliases: how to define a function python
records.definition: A function is a named, reusable block of code. You define it with def, give it a name and optional parameters, and call it by name when needed.
records.explanation:
Defining and calling a function:
    def greet(name):
        return 'Hello, ' + name

    message = greet('Alice')   # 'Hello, Alice'

Key concepts:
- Parameters are the names in the definition. Arguments are the values you pass when calling.
- A function without a return statement returns None.
- Default parameters: def greet(name='World') — used if no argument is given.
- Keyword arguments: greet(name='Bob') — named when calling.
- *args: accept any number of positional arguments.
- **kwargs: accept any number of keyword arguments.

Docstrings — describe what the function does:
    def add(a, b):
        """Return the sum of a and b."""
        return a + b

Scope: variables defined inside a function are local and cannot be accessed outside. Use global keyword to access a global variable, but prefer returning values instead.
common_mistakes: Forgetting return — function returns None silently
Confusing parameter definition with argument passing
Using a mutable default argument like def f(lst=[]) — shared across calls

records.title: Strings in Python
records.definition: A string is a sequence of characters enclosed in single or double quotes. Strings are immutable — you cannot change individual characters, but you can create new strings.
records.explanation:
Creating strings:
    s1 = 'hello'
    s2 = "world"
    s3 = '''multi
    line'''

Common string methods:
    s.upper()          # 'HELLO'
    s.lower()          # 'hello'
    s.strip()          # remove leading/trailing whitespace
    s.split(',')       # split into list by separator
    ','.join(lst)      # join list into string
    s.replace('a','b') # replace all occurrences
    s.find('e')        # index of first match, -1 if not found
    s.startswith('he') # True/False
    len(s)             # length

Indexing and slicing:
    s[0]      # first character
    s[-1]     # last character
    s[1:4]    # characters at index 1, 2, 3
    s[::-1]   # reverse the string

F-strings (Python 3.6+) — the preferred way to format:
    name = 'Alice'
    age = 20
    print(f'Name: {name}, Age: {age}')

Strings are immutable: s[0] = 'H' raises a TypeError.
common_mistakes: Trying to modify a character with indexing assignment
Using + to concatenate in a loop (slow — use join instead)
Forgetting that split() returns a list, not a string

records.title: Lists in Python
records.definition: A list is an ordered, mutable collection of items enclosed in square brackets. Items can be of any type and the list can grow or shrink.
records.explanation:
Creating lists:
    numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    mixed   = [1, 'hello', True, 3.14]
    empty   = []

Common operations:
    numbers[0]         # 1  — first item
    numbers[-1]        # 5  — last item
    numbers[1:3]       # [2, 3]  — slice
    numbers.append(6)  # add to end
    numbers.insert(0, 0) # insert at index
    numbers.pop()      # remove and return last
    numbers.pop(1)     # remove and return index 1
    numbers.remove(3)  # remove first occurrence of value 3
    numbers.sort()     # sort in place
    sorted(numbers)    # return sorted copy
    len(numbers)       # length
    3 in numbers       # True — membership test

List comprehension — concise way to build lists:
    squares = [x**2 for x in range(6)]  # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
    evens   = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]

Lists are mutable: you can change, add, or remove items after creation.
common_mistakes: Confusing index out of range (list has n items; valid indices are 0 to n-1)
Using = to copy a list (creates a reference, not a copy — use lst.copy() or lst[:])
Modifying a list while iterating over it

records.title: Tuples in Python
records.definition: A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence of items enclosed in parentheses. Unlike a list, a tuple cannot be changed after it is created.
records.explanation:
Creating tuples:
    point = (3, 4)
    single = (42,)   # comma is required for single-item tuple
    coords = 1, 2, 3  # parentheses are optional

Accessing items: same indexing and slicing as lists.
    point[0]   # 3
    point[-1]  # 4

Tuple unpacking — assign tuple items to variables:
    x, y = point        # x=3, y=4
    a, *rest = (1,2,3,4) # a=1, rest=[2,3,4]

When to use a tuple over a list:
- When the data should not change (coordinates, RGB colours, database records).
- As dictionary keys (lists cannot be keys because they are mutable).
- Slightly faster than lists for iteration.

Tuples support len(), in, and iteration just like lists, but not append() or sort().
common_mistakes: Forgetting the trailing comma for a single-element tuple: (42) is just 42, not a tuple
Trying to modify a tuple item — raises TypeError

records.title: Sets in Python
records.definition: A set is an unordered collection of unique items enclosed in curly braces. Sets automatically remove duplicates and support fast membership testing.
records.explanation:
Creating sets:
    fruits = {'apple', 'banana', 'apple'}  # {'apple', 'banana'} — duplicate removed
    empty  = set()   # NOT {} — that creates an empty dict

Common operations:
    fruits.add('cherry')        # add one item
    fruits.remove('banana')     # remove (raises error if not found)
    fruits.discard('banana')    # remove safely (no error)
    len(fruits)                 # number of items
    'apple' in fruits           # True — fast membership test

Set operations:
    a | b   # union — all items from both
    a & b   # intersection — items in both
    a - b   # difference — in a but not b
    a ^ b   # symmetric difference — in one but not both

When to use sets:
- Remove duplicates from a list: list(set(my_list))
- Fast membership checking (much faster than a list for large data)
- Mathematical set operations

Sets are unordered — no indexing, no slicing.
common_mistakes: Using {} to create an empty set — this creates an empty dict instead, use set()
Expecting sets to maintain insertion order — they do not

records.title: Dictionaries in Python
records.definition: A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs. Each key maps to exactly one value. Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples). Dictionaries are ordered by insertion order in Python 3.7+.
records.explanation:
Creating dictionaries:
    student = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 20, 'gpa': 3.9}
    empty   = {}

Accessing values:
    student['name']              # 'Alice' — raises KeyError if missing
    student.get('grade', 'N/A')  # safe — returns 'N/A' if key missing

Modifying:
    student['age'] = 21          # update existing key
    student['major'] = 'CS'      # add new key
    del student['gpa']           # delete key

Common methods:
    student.keys()    # all keys
    student.values()  # all values
    student.items()   # (key, value) pairs
    student.update({'age': 22, 'city': 'NY'})  # merge/update
    student.pop('age')  # remove and return value

Iterating:
    for key, value in student.items():
        print(key, value)

Dictionary comprehension:
    squares = {x: x**2 for x in range(5)}
common_mistakes: Using a key that does not exist with [] — use .get() for safety
Using a list as a key — lists are mutable and cannot be dictionary keys

records.title: Input and Output in Python
aliases: how to read user input python
records.definition: Python reads user input with input() and displays output with print(). input() always returns a string — convert it to int or float when needed.
records.explanation:
Displaying output:
    print('Hello, World!')
    print('Sum:', 3 + 4)       # Sum: 7
    print(a, b, sep=', ')     # custom separator
    print('Loading', end='')  # no newline at end

F-string formatting (preferred):
    name = 'Alice'
    age  = 20
    print(f'Name: {name}, Age: {age}')
    print(f'Pi is approximately {3.14159:.2f}')  # 2 decimal places

Reading input:
    name = input('Enter your name: ')   # always a string
    age  = int(input('Enter age: '))    # convert to int
    gpa  = float(input('Enter GPA: '))  # convert to float

Validating input:
    try:
        age = int(input('Enter age: '))
    except ValueError:
        print('Please enter a valid number.')

Reading multiple values on one line:
    a, b = input('Enter two numbers: ').split()
    a, b = int(a), int(b)
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert input() to int or float before arithmetic
Not handling ValueError when the user enters non-numeric text

records.title: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming in Python
records.definition: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. An object is an instance of a class that holds data (attributes) and behaviour (methods). Python supports OOP with the class keyword.
records.explanation:
Defining a class:
```python
    class Student:
        def __init__(self, name, age):
            self.name = name    # instance attribute
            self.age  = age

        def greet(self):
            return f'Hi, I am {self.name}.'
```

Creating objects:
```python
    s1 = Student('Alice', 20)
    s2 = Student('Bob', 22)
    print(s1.greet())   # Hi, I am Alice.
```

Key concepts:
- __init__: the constructor — called automatically when an object is created.
- self: refers to the current object — must be the first parameter of every instance method.
- Attributes: data stored in an object (self.name, self.age).
- Methods: functions defined inside a class.

Inheritance — a subclass inherits from a parent class:
```python
    class GradStudent(Student):
        def __init__(self, name, age, thesis):
            super().__init__(name, age)   # call parent __init__
            self.thesis = thesis
```

The four pillars of OOP:
1. Encapsulation: bundling data and methods together.
2. Inheritance: reusing code from a parent class.
3. Polymorphism: different objects responding to the same method differently.
4. Abstraction: hiding implementation details.
common_mistakes: Forgetting self as the first parameter
Confusing class attributes (shared) with instance attributes (unique per object)
Calling super() incorrectly in __init__

records.title: Errors, Exceptions, and Debugging in Python
records.definition: Python has three kinds of errors: syntax errors (code cannot be parsed), runtime errors (exceptions that occur while running), and logic errors (wrong output but no crash). Use try-except to handle exceptions gracefully.
records.explanation:
Common exception types:
- SyntaxError: invalid Python syntax — caught before running.
- NameError: using a variable that does not exist.
- TypeError: wrong type for an operation (e.g. adding int and str).
- ValueError: right type but invalid value (e.g. int('hello')).
- IndexError: list index out of range.
- KeyError: dictionary key not found.
- ZeroDivisionError: dividing by zero.
- AttributeError: calling a method that does not exist.

Handling exceptions:
    try:
        age = int(input('Enter age: '))
    except ValueError:
        print('Please enter a valid integer.')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'Unexpected error: {e}')
    else:
        print('Input accepted.')   # runs if no exception
    finally:
        print('Done.')             # always runs

Reading a traceback: the last line shows the exception type and message. The lines above show the call stack — read from bottom to top to find where the error occurred.

Raising exceptions:
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError('Age cannot be negative.')
common_mistakes: Catching a bare except without specifying the type — hides real bugs
Not reading the traceback carefully — the error is usually on or near the last line shown

records.title: Modules and Imports in Python
records.definition: A module is a Python file containing functions, classes, and variables you can reuse in other files. Use import to bring a module into your script.
records.explanation:
Importing a module:
    import math
    print(math.sqrt(16))   # 4.0
    print(math.pi)         # 3.14159...

Importing specific items:
    from math import sqrt, pi
    print(sqrt(25))        # 5.0 — no math. prefix needed

Importing with an alias:
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd

Useful standard library modules:
- math: sqrt, pow, floor, ceil, pi, e
- random: random(), randint(), choice(), shuffle()
- os: file system operations
- sys: interpreter information
- datetime: dates and times
- json: read/write JSON data
- re: regular expressions
- collections: Counter, defaultdict, deque

Creating your own module: save a .py file and import it by filename (without .py).

Packages: a folder containing an __init__.py file and multiple modules.

The main guard:
    if __name__ == '__main__':
        main()
This code runs only when the file is executed directly, not when imported.
common_mistakes: Importing a module name that conflicts with a built-in name
Forgetting the main guard when a module also has runnable code

records.title: Scope in Python
records.definition: Scope determines where a variable is accessible. Python uses the LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in — it searches in that order.
records.explanation:
Local scope: a variable defined inside a function is local to that function.
    def greet():
        message = 'Hello'   # local
        print(message)
    greet()
    # print(message)  # NameError — not accessible here

Global scope: a variable defined at the top level is global.
    total = 0
    def add(n):
        global total
        total += n   # global keyword required to modify

Enclosing scope: relevant for nested functions. Use nonlocal to modify a variable in the enclosing function.

LEGB lookup order:
1. Local — variables inside the current function
2. Enclosing — variables in outer (but not global) functions
3. Global — top-level module variables
4. Built-in — Python built-ins like len, print, range

Best practice: avoid modifying global variables from inside functions. Pass values as parameters and return results instead.
common_mistakes: Trying to modify a global variable without the global keyword — creates a new local variable instead
Shadowing built-in names (e.g. naming a variable list or len)

records.title: Recursion in Python
records.definition: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function must have a base case that stops the recursion.
records.explanation:
Structure of a recursive function:
    def factorial(n):
        if n == 0:          # base case — stops recursion
            return 1
        return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive call

    print(factorial(5))   # 120

How it works (factorial(3)):
    factorial(3) → 3 * factorial(2)
                    → 3 * 2 * factorial(1)
                          → 3 * 2 * 1 * factorial(0)
                                    → 3 * 2 * 1 * 1 = 6

Fibonacci example:
    def fib(n):
        if n <= 1:
            return n
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

Python's default recursion limit is 1000 calls. You can check it with sys.getrecursionlimit().

When to use recursion vs iteration:
- Recursion is natural for problems with self-similar substructure (trees, factorials, Fibonacci).
- Iteration is generally more memory-efficient for simple loops.
common_mistakes: Missing the base case — causes infinite recursion and RecursionError
Base case condition is wrong and recursion never terminates

records.title: Indentation in Python
records.definition: Python uses indentation (spaces at the start of a line) to define code blocks instead of curly braces. The standard is 4 spaces per level.
records.explanation:
In most languages, curly braces { } define code blocks. Python uses indentation:
    if x > 0:
        print('positive')    # 4 spaces — inside the if block
        print('still inside')
    print('outside block')   # 0 spaces — outside

Rules:
- Consistent indentation is required — mixing tabs and spaces causes IndentationError.
- The standard (PEP 8) is 4 spaces per level.
- All lines in the same block must have the same indentation.

Nested blocks add another 4 spaces:
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            print(i, j)   # 8 spaces deep

IndentationError means your code is inconsistently indented. Check that you have not mixed tabs and spaces — configure your editor to use spaces.

Inconsistent number of spaces in the same block

quick_facts.value: Executes Java bytecode on any platform

quick_facts.label: JDK vs JRE vs JVM

records.definition: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is a virtual engine that **runs Java bytecode on any operating system**, enabling 'Write Once, Run Anywhere'.
records.explanation:
How Java runs your code:
1. You write .java source code
2. javac (Java compiler) converts it to .class bytecode files
3. The JVM on the target machine reads and executes the bytecode
4. The JVM translates bytecode to native machine instructions at runtime

This means the same .class file runs unchanged on Windows, macOS, and Linux — as long as a JVM is installed. The JVM also handles memory management through garbage collection.
records.fun_fact: The JVM is so well-designed that other languages like Kotlin, Scala, and Groovy also compile to Java bytecode and run on the JVM.

records.title: How Does Java Compile and Run?

quick_facts.label: Step 1
quick_facts.value: Write source code in a .java file

quick_facts.label: Step 2
quick_facts.value: Compile with javac: javac Hello.java → Hello.class

quick_facts.label: Execution
quick_facts.value: JVM interprets bytecode at runtime (with JIT compilation)

records.definition: Java is **compiled to bytecode** (not machine code), which the JVM then executes — combining compilation benefits with platform independence.
records.explanation:
Java's two-step execution process:

1. Compile: javac Hello.java → creates Hello.class (bytecode)
2. Run: java Hello → JVM loads and executes the bytecode

Java uses Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation — the JVM compiles frequently-used bytecode to native machine code at runtime for performance. This makes Java faster than pure interpreters while remaining platform-independent.

Compare with Python (purely interpreted) and C (compiled directly to machine code).
records.fun_fact: Java's JIT compiler can actually make some Java programs run as fast as C — because it can optimize code based on actual runtime behaviour.

records.title: The Java main Method and Program Structure
aliases: how to write a java program
records.definition: Every Java program starts execution from the main method. It must be declared as: public static void main(String[] args) inside a class.
records.explanation:
Minimal Java program:
    public class HelloWorld {
        public static void main(String[] args) {
            System.out.println("Hello, World!");
        }
    }

Breaking down the main method signature:
- public: accessible from anywhere — the JVM needs to call it.
- static: belongs to the class, not an object — the JVM does not create an object first.
- void: returns nothing.
- main: the name the JVM looks for to start execution.
- String[] args: command-line arguments passed to the program (can be an empty array).

System.out.println prints a line and moves to the next line.
System.out.print prints without a newline.
System.out.printf prints with C-style format specifiers.

Every Java source file must:
- Have the same name as the public class it contains (HelloWorld.java for class HelloWorld).
- Contain exactly one public class.
- End with .java.

Compiling and running:
    javac HelloWorld.java   // creates HelloWorld.class
    java HelloWorld         // runs the class
common_mistakes: Wrong main signature (missing static or wrong parameter type)
File name does not match the public class name
Calling System.out.println without the semicolon

records.title: Variables and Data Types in Java
records.definition: Java requires you to declare the type of every variable before using it. The main primitive types are int, double, char, and boolean. String is a class, not a primitive.
records.explanation:
Primitive types:
    int     age    = 20;        // whole number, 32-bit
    long    pop    = 8_000_000L; // large whole number, 64-bit
    double  gpa    = 3.9;       // decimal number, 64-bit
    float   pi     = 3.14f;     // decimal, 32-bit (needs f suffix)
    char    grade  = 'A';       // single character, 16-bit
    boolean passed = true;      // true or false
    byte    b      = 127;       // small integer, 8-bit
    short   s      = 32000;     // small integer, 16-bit

String (reference type):
    String name = "Alice";   // double quotes only

Type casting:
    double d = 9.7;
    int    i = (int) d;      // explicit cast: i = 9 (truncated)

    int x  = 5;
    double y = x;            // implicit widening: y = 5.0

Wrapper classes — each primitive has an object equivalent:
    Integer, Double, Character, Boolean
Used when a primitive is needed as an object (e.g. in collections).
    Integer.parseInt("42")   // String to int
    String.valueOf(42)       // int to String

Constants (final keyword):
    final double PI = 3.14159;   // cannot be reassigned
common_mistakes: Forgetting that integer division truncates: 7/2 = 3, not 3.5
Using == to compare Strings (compares references, not content — use .equals())
Missing the L suffix for long literals larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE

records.title: Operators in Java
records.definition: Java supports arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, and bitwise operators. Integer division truncates the result. Use cast to double for decimal division.
records.explanation:
Arithmetic:
    +  -  *  /  %   (modulo)
    7 / 2 = 3        // integer division — truncates
    7 / 2.0 = 3.5    // at least one double gives double result
    7 % 2 = 1        // remainder

Increment/decrement:
    x++   // post-increment: use then add 1
    ++x   // pre-increment:  add 1 then use
    x--   // post-decrement

Comparison (return boolean):
    ==  !=  <  >  <=  >=
    NOTE: use .equals() for String comparison, not ==

Logical:
    &&   // AND (short-circuit)
    ||   // OR  (short-circuit)
    !    // NOT

Assignment:
    =  +=  -=  *=  /=  %=

Ternary:
    int max = (a > b) ? a : b;

Operator precedence (highest first):
    ++/-- (post) → ++/-- (pre), unary - → * / % → + - → comparisons → ! → && → || → ternary → assignment
common_mistakes: Integer division: int/int always gives int
Using == on String objects instead of .equals()
Confusing x++ (post) and ++x (pre) in expressions

records.title: Conditional Statements in Java
records.definition: Java uses if, else if, and else for conditional execution, and switch for matching a value against multiple cases.
common_mistakes: Forgetting break in switch — causes fall-through to next case
Using = instead of == in condition
Missing semicolons inside switch cases

records.title: Loops in Java

Infinite loop by forgetting to update loop variable
Modifying collection while iterating with for-each (use Iterator instead)

records.title: Methods in Java

common_mistakes: Expecting a primitive to be modified inside a method (primitives are passed by value)
Confusing static and instance methods — calling instance method from static context

records.title: Classes and Objects in Java

common_mistakes: Forgetting to use this. when a field and parameter share a name
Calling an instance method without creating an object first

records.title: Access Modifiers in Java

Forgetting that private fields are not accessible in subclasses (use protected or getters)

records.title: Inheritance in Java
records.definition: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend the fields and methods of a superclass. Use the extends keyword. Java supports single inheritance — one class can extend only one other class.

Calling super() after other code in the constructor — it must be the first statement

common_mistakes: Not implementing all methods of an interface — compile error
Trying to instantiate an interface or abstract class directly

records.title: Arrays in Java
records.definition: An array in Java is a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same type. The size is set when the array is created and cannot change.
common_mistakes: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: accessing index >= array.length
Confusing array.length (field, no parentheses) with String.length() (method, needs parentheses)
Assigning one array to another with = copies the reference, not the content

records.title: Collections in Java — ArrayList and HashMap
records.definition: The Java Collections Framework provides resizable and flexible data structures. ArrayList is a resizable list; HashMap stores key-value pairs. Both use generics to specify element types.
common_mistakes: Using int in ArrayList<int> — must use Integer
ConcurrentModificationException when removing from a list inside a for-each loop
keywords: what is a list in java

records.title: Exception Handling in Java
records.definition: Java uses exceptions to signal errors at runtime. Use try-catch to handle them. Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked exceptions do not.
common_mistakes: Catching Exception and silently swallowing it — hides the real problem
Forgetting that finally always runs — do not use return inside it if you rely on the value

records.title: Strings in Java
records.definition: In Java, String is a class, not a primitive type. Strings are immutable — once created, their content cannot be changed. Use .equals() to compare Strings, not ==.
records.explanation:
Creating strings:
    String s1 = "Hello";          // string literal (preferred)
    String s2 = new String("Hi"); // creates a new object

Common methods:
    s1.length()          // 5
    s1.charAt(0)         // 'H'
    s1.toUpperCase()     // "HELLO"
    s1.toLowerCase()     // "hello"
    s1.substring(1, 3)   // "el" (index 1 inclusive, 3 exclusive)
    s1.contains("ell")   // true
    s1.replace('l','r')  // "Herro"
    s1.trim()            // remove leading/trailing whitespace
    s1.split(", ")        // split into String[]
    s1.indexOf('l')      // 2 — first occurrence
    s1.equals("Hello")  // true — correct comparison
    s1.equalsIgnoreCase("hello")  // true

String concatenation:
    String full = "Hello" + " " + "World";  // concatenation
    String msg  = "Age: " + 20;             // auto-converts int

StringBuilder — mutable string for building in a loop:
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) sb.append(i);
    String result = sb.toString();   // "01234"

Why == fails for strings:
    String a = new String("hi");
    String b = new String("hi");
    a == b       // false — different objects
    a.equals(b)  // true  — same content
common_mistakes: Using == to compare strings instead of .equals()
Calling methods on a null String — causes NullPointerException

records.title: Input and Output in Java
records.definition: Java reads input from the keyboard using the Scanner class and prints output using System.out.println. Import java.util.Scanner before using it.
common_mistakes: Not consuming the leftover newline after nextInt() before calling nextLine()
Forgetting the import statement for Scanner

records.title: Scope in Java
records.definition: Scope defines where a variable is accessible. Java has local scope (inside a method), instance scope (inside an object), and class scope (static, shared across all objects).
common_mistakes: Using a local variable before initialising it — Java requires explicit initialisation
Confusing an instance variable with a local variable when names match — use this.

records.title: Recursion in Java
records.definition: Recursion in Java is when a method calls itself. Every recursive method needs a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that reduces the problem.
common_mistakes: Missing base case — causes StackOverflowError
Base case condition is wrong and recursion never terminates

records.title: Packages and Imports in Java
records.definition: A package is a namespace that organises related classes. The import statement brings classes from other packages into your file so you can use them without the full package name.
records.explanation:
Declaring a package (first line of file):
    package com.myapp.models;

Importing a specific class:
    import java.util.Scanner;
    import java.util.ArrayList;

Importing all classes from a package:
    import java.util.*;

Commonly used packages:
    java.util    — Scanner, ArrayList, HashMap, Arrays, Collections
    java.lang    — String, Math, Integer, System (auto-imported)
    java.io      — file I/O
    java.math    — BigDecimal, BigInteger

Math class (no import needed — in java.lang):
    Math.abs(-5)         // 5
    Math.sqrt(16)        // 4.0
    Math.pow(2, 10)      // 1024.0
    Math.max(3, 7)       // 7
    Math.min(3, 7)       // 3
    Math.random()        // 0.0 to < 1.0
    Math.floor(3.9)      // 3.0
    Math.ceil(3.1)       // 4.0
    Math.round(3.5)      // 4
common_mistakes: Forgetting to import Scanner before using it
Importing java.util.* when you only need one class — works but is less explicit

C is compiled directly to machine code — there is no virtual machine or interpreter between your code and the CPU. This makes C extremely fast and efficient.

Core characteristics of C:
- Procedural: code is organised into functions (no classes)

- Portable: same code compiles for any platform

BCPL (1967) → B (1969) → C (1972)

- BCPL: Martin Richards' language, used at MIT
- B: Ken Thompson simplified BCPL for the PDP-7 at Bell Labs
- C: Dennis Ritchie added data types to B and improved it for the PDP-11

The key improvement C made over B: B was a 'typeless' language — it treated all data as machine words. C added int, char, float and a proper type system, making it much more expressive and safer for system programming.

quick_facts.label: No VM needed
quick_facts.value: Unlike Java, C has no Virtual Machine

records.definition: C is a **compiled language** — source code is converted directly to native machine code by a compiler (like GCC or Clang), then executed directly by the CPU.
records.explanation:
C's execution process:

1. Write: hello.c source file
2. Compile: gcc hello.c -o hello
   - Preprocessor: handles #include and #define
   - Compiler: converts C to assembly
   - Assembler: converts assembly to object code (.o)
   - Linker: combines object files + libraries → executable
3. Run: ./hello — the CPU executes machine code directly

No interpreter, no virtual machine, no bytecode — the compiled output IS the final program. This is why C programs are so fast.
records.fun_fact: A C program compiled on an x86 processor cannot run on an ARM processor without recompilation — unlike Java which runs the same bytecode everywhere.

records.title: The main Function and Program Structure in C
records.definition: Every C program must have a main function — this is where execution begins. The standard signature is int main(void) or int main(int argc, char *argv[]). It returns 0 to signal success.
common_mistakes: Using void main() instead of int main(void) — not standard C
Forgetting #include <stdio.h> when using printf or scanf
Forgetting return 0 at the end (required in C89; optional in C99+)

records.title: Header Files and the Preprocessor in C
records.definition: Header files (.h files) declare functions, types, and constants from libraries. Use #include to bring them into your file. The #define directive creates constants and macros.
common_mistakes: Forgetting #include <stdio.h> before using printf/scanf
Macro without parentheses: #define SQ(x) x*x gives wrong result for SQ(2+3)

records.title: Variables and Data Types in C
records.definition: C requires you to declare the type of every variable before using it. Basic types include int, float, double, and char. C is statically typed and does not initialise variables automatically.
records.explanation:
Basic types:
    int    age    = 20;        // integer, typically 32-bit
    long   pop    = 8000000L;  // larger integer, typically 64-bit
    float  pi     = 3.14f;    // single-precision decimal
    double gpa    = 3.9;      // double-precision decimal (preferred)
    char   grade  = 'A';      // single character (stored as integer)
    _Bool  flag   = 1;        // 0 = false, 1 = true (C99)

Signed vs unsigned:
    unsigned int u = 300;   // only non-negative values
    signed int   s = -50;   // positive and negative

Checking sizes:
    sizeof(int)      // typically 4 bytes
    sizeof(double)   // typically 8 bytes
    sizeof(char)     // always 1 byte

Type casting:
    int a = 7, b = 2;
    double result = (double)a / b;  // 3.5 — explicit cast
    int   trunc   = (int)3.9;       // 3   — truncation

Constants:
    #define MAX 100           // preprocessor constant
    const int LIMIT = 100;    // type-safe constant (preferred)

Important: C does NOT initialise local variables automatically. An uninitialised variable holds whatever garbage value was previously in that memory location.
common_mistakes: Using an uninitialised variable — undefined behaviour
Integer division losing the decimal part: 7/2 = 3, not 3.5
Forgetting that char is really a small integer (its ASCII value)

records.title: Format Specifiers in C (printf and scanf)
records.definition: Format specifiers tell printf how to display a value and scanf what type to read. Each type has its own specifier: %d for int, %f for float/double, %c for char, %s for strings.
records.explanation:
Common format specifiers:
    %d   — int (decimal integer)
    %ld  — long int
    %f   — float or double (default 6 decimal places)
    %lf  — double in scanf
    %c   — char (single character)
    %s   — string (char array)
    %p   — pointer (memory address)
    %x   — hexadecimal integer
    %o   — octal integer
    %%   — literal % sign

Printf examples:
    printf("%d\n", 42);           // 42
    printf("%.2f\n", 3.14159);    // 3.14  (2 decimal places)
    printf("%10d\n", 42);         //         42  (right-aligned, width 10)
    printf("%-10d|\n", 42);       // 42        | (left-aligned)
    printf("%05d\n", 42);         // 00042  (zero-padded)
    printf("%c\n", 'A');          // A
    printf("%s\n", "hello");      // hello

Scanf — always use the address-of operator & with non-string variables:
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);         // read integer into n
    double d;
    scanf("%lf", &d);        // read double (use %lf not %f in scanf)
    char name[50];
    scanf("%s", name);       // read word (no & needed for arrays)
    scanf("%49s", name);     // limit to 49 characters for safety

Escape sequences in strings:
    \n  — newline
    \t  — tab
    \\  — backslash
    \"  — double quote
common_mistakes: Using %f instead of %lf in scanf for double
Forgetting & in scanf (except for strings/arrays)
Mismatching format specifier and variable type — causes undefined behaviour

records.title: Operators in C
records.definition: C supports arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, bitwise, and sizeof operators. Integer division truncates. Logical operators return 0 (false) or 1 (true).
records.explanation:
Arithmetic:
    +  -  *  /  %
    7 / 2 = 3      // integer division — truncates
    7 % 2 = 1      // remainder (modulo)
    (double)7 / 2 = 3.5  // cast to get decimal result

Increment/decrement:
    x++  // post-increment: use value then increment
    ++x  // pre-increment:  increment then use
    x--  // post-decrement

Comparison (return 0 or 1):
    ==  !=  <  >  <=  >=
    C has no boolean type before C99 — 0 is false, any non-zero is true.

Logical:
    &&  — AND (short-circuit)
    ||  — OR  (short-circuit)
    !   — NOT

Bitwise:
    &   — AND
    |   — OR
    ^   — XOR
    ~   — NOT
    <<  — left shift
    >>  — right shift

Assignment:
    =  +=  -=  *=  /=  %=  &=  |=  ^=  <<=  >>=

Sizeof:
    sizeof(int)      // size in bytes at compile time
    sizeof(x)        // size of variable x

Ternary:
    int max = (a > b) ? a : b;

Precedence (highest first): () → ++ -- (post) → * / % → + - → << >> → comparisons → == != → & → ^ → | → && → || → ternary → assignment
common_mistakes: Using = instead of == in conditions (assignment, not comparison)
Integer division losing decimal: 7/2 = 3 — cast one operand to double
Using && instead of & or vice versa (logical vs bitwise)

records.title: Conditional Statements in C
records.definition: C uses if, else if, and else for conditional execution, and switch for matching an integer expression against multiple cases.
common_mistakes: Using = instead of == in condition — common in C (silently assigns and evaluates)
Forgetting break in switch — causes fall-through
Testing floats for exact equality — use a small tolerance instead

records.title: Loops in C
records.definition: C has three loop types: for (count-controlled), while (condition-controlled), and do-while (runs at least once). break exits a loop; continue skips to the next iteration.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one: using <= when the array index goes from 0 to n-1
Infinite loop by forgetting to update the loop variable
Using i < sizeof(arr) instead of i < n (sizeof gives bytes, not element count)

records.title: Functions in C
records.definition: A function in C is a named, reusable block of code. It has a return type, a name, and optional parameters. C uses pass-by-value — a copy of each argument is passed.
common_mistakes: Expecting a primitive value to be modified in the caller without using a pointer
Calling a function before declaring it — causes implicit declaration warning/error
Returning a pointer to a local variable — that memory is freed when the function returns
keywords: how to define a function in c

records.title: Arrays in C
records.definition: An array in C is a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory holding elements of the same type. Arrays are zero-indexed. The size must be known at compile time (or allocated with malloc at runtime).
common_mistakes: Accessing index out of bounds — undefined behaviour, no error in C
Using sizeof(arr) instead of sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) to get count
Assuming the array is passed by value to a function — it decays to a pointer

records.title: Strings in C
records.definition: In C, a string is an array of characters ending with a null terminator character '\0'. There is no built-in string type. Use char arrays and functions from string.h.
records.explanation:
Creating strings:
    char greeting[] = "Hello";        // size = 6: H e l l o \0
    char name[50];                     // uninitialized buffer
    char name[50] = {0};               // zero-initialized (safe)

The null terminator \0 marks the end. String functions rely on it.

Common string functions (require #include <string.h>):
    strlen(s)             // length NOT including \0
    strcpy(dest, src)     // copy src into dest
    strncpy(dest,src,n)   // copy at most n chars (safer)
    strcat(dest, src)     // append src to dest
    strncat(dest,src,n)   // append at most n chars
    strcmp(a, b)          // 0 if equal, <0 if a<b, >0 if a>b
    strncmp(a,b,n)        // compare first n characters
    strchr(s, 'c')        // pointer to first occurrence of 'c'
    strstr(s, "sub")      // pointer to first occurrence of substring

Reading strings:
    scanf("%49s", name);       // reads one word, max 49 chars
    fgets(name, 50, stdin);    // reads full line (safer)

Comparing strings — use strcmp, not ==:
    if (strcmp(a, b) == 0) { ... }   // correct
    if (a == b) { ... }              // compares addresses, not content!

String literals are read-only:
    char *s = "hello";   // pointer to read-only memory
    s[0] = 'H';          // undefined behaviour — do not do this
    char s[] = "hello";  // this copy is writable
common_mistakes: Using == to compare strings instead of strcmp
Buffer overflow: writing more characters than the array can hold
Forgetting the null terminator when building a string manually

records.title: Pointers in C
records.definition: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Use & to get an address and * to dereference (access the value at that address).
records.explanation:
Basic pointer usage:
    int x = 42;
    int *p = &x;    // p stores the address of x

    printf("%d\n", *p);   // 42 — dereference: value at address
    *p = 100;             // change x through the pointer
    printf("%d\n", x);    // 100

Pointer to pointer:
    int **pp = &p;  // pointer to a pointer

Null pointer — a pointer that points to nothing:
    int *p = NULL;  // always initialise to NULL if not assigning
    if (p != NULL) { ... }  // always check before dereferencing

Pointer arithmetic:
    int arr[] = {10, 20, 30};
    int *p = arr;      // points to arr[0]
    p++;               // now points to arr[1]
    printf("%d\n", *p); // 20

Passing by pointer to modify a value:
    void swap(int *a, int *b) {
        int temp = *a;
        *a = *b;
        *b = temp;
    }
    int x = 3, y = 5;
    swap(&x, &y);   // x=5, y=3

Pointers and arrays:
    arr[i] == *(arr + i)  // equivalent — pointer arithmetic

Common pointer types:
    int *p    — pointer to int
    char *s   — pointer to char (often used for strings)
    void *vp  — generic pointer (no type — must cast before use)
common_mistakes: Dereferencing a null or uninitialised pointer — segmentation fault
Forgetting & when passing a variable to scanf or a swap function
Returning a pointer to a local variable — the memory is freed when the function returns

records.title: Structures (struct) in C
records.definition: A struct groups related variables of different types under one name. It is C's way of creating a custom data type — similar to a class in Java or Python, but without methods.
common_mistakes: Using the dot operator on a pointer (need ->)
Forgetting to allocate enough space in char arrays for strings including \0
Assigning one struct to another with = copies all fields (but does NOT deep-copy pointer members)
keywords: what is a record in c

records.title: Memory Management in C
records.definition: C requires you to manage heap memory manually. Use malloc to allocate memory, and free to release it. Forgetting to free allocated memory causes a memory leak.
records.explanation:
Stack vs Heap:
- Stack: memory for local variables — automatically managed, limited size.
- Heap: dynamically allocated memory — you control when it is created and freed.

Allocating memory:
    #include <stdlib.h>

    int *arr = malloc(5 * sizeof(int));   // allocate 5 ints
    if (arr == NULL) {                     // always check!
        fprintf(stderr, "Allocation failed\n");
        exit(1);
    }
    arr[0] = 10;   // use like a regular array

calloc — allocate AND zero-initialise:
    int *arr = calloc(5, sizeof(int));   // 5 ints, all set to 0

realloc — resize an existing allocation:
    arr = realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int));  // grow to 10 ints

Free when done:
    free(arr);
    arr = NULL;   // good practice — prevents use-after-free

Common memory errors:
- Memory leak: allocated memory never freed.
- Use-after-free: accessing memory after free().
- Double-free: calling free() on the same pointer twice.
- Buffer overflow: writing past the end of an allocated block.
- Dangling pointer: pointer still holds address of freed memory.

Tools to detect errors: Valgrind (Linux/macOS), AddressSanitizer.
common_mistakes: Not checking if malloc returned NULL
Forgetting to call free() — causes memory leak
Using the pointer after calling free() — undefined behaviour

records.title: Input and Output in C
records.definition: C uses printf for output and scanf or fgets for input, both declared in stdio.h. scanf reads formatted input; fgets reads a full line safely.
common_mistakes: Using scanf("%s") for input with spaces — use fgets instead
Not consuming leftover newline between scanf and fgets calls
Forgetting & in scanf for non-array variables

records.title: Common Errors and Debugging in C
records.definition: C has compile-time errors (syntax, type issues), runtime errors (segfault, invalid memory access), and logic errors (wrong output). C does not throw exceptions — errors often cause silent undefined behaviour or crashes.
records.explanation:
Compile-time errors:
- Syntax errors: missing semicolon, unmatched braces.
- Undeclared variables/functions: use before declaring.
- Type mismatch: assigning incompatible types without cast.
- Missing return statement in non-void function.

Runtime errors:
- Segmentation fault: accessing memory you do not own (null pointer, out-of-bounds array, freed memory).
- Stack overflow: infinite recursion exhausting the call stack.
- Division by zero: dividing an integer by 0.
- Memory leak: allocated memory never freed (program does not crash, but wastes RAM).

Logic errors: program compiles and runs but produces wrong output.
Example: using = instead of == in a condition.

Debugging strategies:
1. Read the compiler warning messages — enable all with gcc -Wall -Wextra.
2. Add printf statements to trace variable values.
3. Use a debugger: gdb (Linux/macOS) or the IDE debugger.
4. Check array bounds manually.
5. Check all pointers for NULL before dereferencing.
6. Use Valgrind to detect memory errors.

Common error messages:
    'implicit declaration of function': forgot #include or prototype.
    'incompatible types': type mismatch in assignment.
    'expected expression': syntax error nearby.
    Segmentation fault: memory access violation at runtime.

records.title: Scope in C
records.definition: Scope in C determines where a variable is accessible. C has block scope (inside {}), function scope, file scope (global), and program scope. Static variables persist across function calls.
common_mistakes: Using an uninitialised local variable — undefined behaviour
Relying on global variables across many functions — makes code hard to debug

records.title: Recursion in C
records.definition: Recursion in C is when a function calls itself. Every recursive function must have a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that moves toward it.
common_mistakes: Missing base case — causes infinite recursion and stack overflow
Not reducing the problem toward the base case in each call

records.title: Variables Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: All three languages use variables to store data, but they differ in how types are declared. Python uses dynamic typing (no declaration needed), Java uses static typing (type required), and C uses static typing with manual memory concerns.
records.explanation:
Python — dynamic typing:
    name = 'Alice'    # no type declaration
    age  = 20         # Python infers int
    age  = 'twenty'   # can change type — allowed

Java — static typing:
    String name = "Alice";   // type is required
    int    age  = 20;        // cannot later assign a String to age

C — static typing:
    char name[50] = "Alice";  // fixed-size char array
    int  age      = 20;       // uninitialized local variables contain garbage

Key differences:
| Feature              | Python        | Java           | C              |
|----------------------|---------------|----------------|----------------|
| Type declaration     | Not needed    | Required       | Required       |
| Type can change      | Yes           | No             | No             |
| Default value        | N/A (must assign) | 0/null/false (fields) | Undefined (local) |
| String type          | str (built-in)| String (class) | char array     |
| Boolean type         | bool          | boolean        | int (0/1) or _Bool |
| Null/empty concept   | None          | null           | NULL (pointer) |
common_mistakes: Expecting C local variables to be 0 by default like Java instance fields
Forgetting that Python strings are immutable but Java Strings also are, while C char arrays are mutable

records.title: Loops Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: All three languages support for and while loops, but their syntax differs significantly. Python's for loop iterates over sequences; Java and C use a three-part for loop with initialiser, condition, and update.
common_mistakes: Expecting Python's range(1,6) to include 6 — it stops at 5
Forgetting curly braces in Java/C for multi-line loop bodies

records.title: Functions/Methods Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: All three languages support reusable named code blocks. Python uses def with no type declarations; Java uses methods inside classes with explicit types; C uses functions with explicit types and requires prototypes.
common_mistakes: Thinking Python passes all values by value — mutable objects like lists are passed by reference
Forgetting Java methods must be inside a class

records.title: Strings Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: Python and Java have built-in String types that are immutable. C has no string type — strings are char arrays terminated by a null character. Comparing and manipulating strings works very differently across the three languages.
records.explanation:
Creating strings:
    Python:  name = 'Alice'
    Java:    String name = "Alice";
    C:       char name[] = "Alice";   // or char name[50];

Getting length:
    Python:  len(name)          # 5
    Java:    name.length()      // 5
    C:       strlen(name)       // 5  (requires string.h)

Comparing strings:
    Python:  name == 'Alice'      # True  — built-in comparison
    Java:    name.equals("Alice") // true  — use .equals(), NOT ==
    C:       strcmp(name,"Alice") == 0  // 0 means equal

Concatenation:
    Python:  full = first + ' ' + last
    Java:    String full = first + " " + last;  // or StringBuilder
    C:       strcat(first, last);  // modifies first in place — must have space!

Immutability:
    Python:  Strings are immutable — s[0] = 'H' raises TypeError
    Java:    Strings are immutable — use StringBuilder for heavy modification
    C:       char arrays are mutable — you can modify individual characters

Key insight for C: always include the null terminator in size calculations:
    char name[6] = "Alice";  // 5 chars + 1 for '\0'
common_mistakes: Using == for string comparison in Java (compares references, not content)
Using == for string comparison in C (compares addresses, not content)

records.title: Arrays and Collections Compared: Python vs Java vs C
aliases: python list java array c array
records.definition: Python uses lists (dynamic, any type), Java offers fixed arrays and ArrayList (dynamic), and C has fixed-size arrays. Python lists and Java ArrayList grow automatically; C arrays do not.
records.explanation:
Creating and initialising:
    Python:  nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]        # dynamic, any type
    Java:    int[] nums = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; // fixed-size array
             ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(); // dynamic
    C:       int nums[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; // fixed-size array

Adding elements:
    Python:  nums.append(6)                # built-in
    Java:    list.add(6);                  // ArrayList only
    C:       // not possible with static array — use realloc for dynamic

Accessing by index:
    Python:  nums[0]   # 1
    Java:    nums[0]   // 1
    C:       nums[0]   // 1

Length:
    Python:  len(nums)                              # 5
    Java:    nums.length  (array) / list.size()     // 5
    C:       sizeof(nums)/sizeof(nums[0])           // 5 (only in scope)

Key differences:
| Feature          | Python list  | Java array   | Java ArrayList | C array     |
|------------------|-------------|--------------|----------------|-------------|
| Size fixed?      | No           | Yes          | No             | Yes         |
| Mixed types?     | Yes          | No           | No             | No          |
| Bounds checking  | Yes (raises) | Yes (throws) | Yes (throws)   | No (UB)     |
| Negative index   | Yes          | No           | No             | No          |
common_mistakes: Accessing out-of-bounds index in C — no exception, just undefined behaviour
Using Python's negative indexing in Java or C — it does not work there

records.title: Object-Oriented Programming Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: Python and Java are object-oriented languages with full class support. C is procedural — it does not support classes or inheritance, but structs can group related data.
common_mistakes: Expecting C structs to have methods — they do not
Forgetting self in Python method definitions
keywords: what is a class in programming

records.title: Error Handling Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: Python and Java use exception handling with try-except/catch blocks. C has no exceptions — errors must be checked manually through return values and errno.
common_mistakes: Expecting C to throw an exception on array out-of-bounds — it silently causes undefined behaviour
Not checking return values of C library functions like malloc, scanf, fopen
keywords: error handling in python java c

records.title: Input and Output Compared: Python vs Java vs C
records.definition: All three languages support reading keyboard input and printing to the console, but the syntax and functions differ. Python uses print() and input(); Java uses System.out.println() and Scanner; C uses printf() and scanf().
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert Python input() from string to int
Forgetting & in C scanf for non-array variables
Scanner newline issue in Java after nextInt()
keywords: input output in python java c

records.title: Overview of Python, Java, and C — History and Comparison
records.definition: Python, Java, and C are three of the most widely used programming languages. Each was created for different purposes, in different eras, and with different design philosophies.
records.explanation:
Quick reference:

| Property          | Python (1991)      | Java (1995)         | C (1972)             |
|-------------------|--------------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Creator           | Guido van Rossum   | James Gosling        | Dennis Ritchie       |
| Origin            | CWI, Netherlands   | Sun Microsystems     | Bell Labs, USA       |
| Paradigm          | Multi (OOP, proc, func) | OOP           | Procedural           |
| Execution         | Interpreted        | Compiled to bytecode (JVM) | Compiled to native |
| Typing            | Dynamic            | Static               | Static               |
| Memory management | Automatic (GC)     | Automatic (GC)       | Manual (malloc/free) |
| Primary use today | Data science, web, AI | Enterprise, Android | OS, embedded, systems |
| Beginner friendly | High               | Medium               | Low                  |

Why learn all three:
- C teaches how computers actually work (memory, pointers, compilation).
- Java teaches strict object-oriented thinking and enterprise patterns.
- Python teaches rapid prototyping, readability, and modern data/AI workflows.

Order recommendation for beginners: Python first (readable, forgiving), then Java (introduces strict typing and OOP), then C (deepens understanding of memory and systems).

quick_facts.label: What it is
quick_facts.value: An isolated Python workspace with its own packages

records.definition: A **virtual environment** is an isolated folder that contains its own Python interpreter and packages — separate from other projects on the same computer.
records.explanation:
Why you need a virtual environment:
Without a venv, every project on your computer shares the same packages. If Project A needs Flask 2.0 and Project B needs Flask 3.0, they will conflict.

A venv solves this by giving each project its own private package folder.

Key commands:
  Create:           python -m venv venv
  Activate Windows: venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
  Activate Mac/Linux: source venv/bin/activate
  Deactivate:       deactivate

When a venv is active, your terminal prompt changes to show (venv) at the start.
Every pip install you run while active goes into that venv only.

Note: Only Python supports virtual environments among Python, Java, and C.
Java uses Maven/Gradle for dependency management.
C uses system libraries and Makefiles — no package isolation system.
records.fun_fact: The venv folder in this project is called .venv — the dot makes it hidden on macOS/Linux. You can name your venv anything: venv, .venv, env, myproject.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to activate the venv before running pip install
Committing the venv folder to Git — add it to .gitignore instead
Creating a new venv inside another venv

records.title: pip — Python Package Installer
keywords: how to install packages using pip
how to install a package using pip
records.definition: **pip** (Pip Installs Packages) is Python's official package manager — it downloads and installs third-party libraries from the Python Package Index (PyPI).
records.explanation:
Common pip commands:

  Install a package:
    pip install flask
    pip install numpy pandas matplotlib

  Install a specific version:
    pip install flask==3.0.0

  Remove a package:
    pip uninstall flask

  See all installed packages:
    pip list

  See details about one package:
    pip show flask

  Save your installed packages to a file:
    pip freeze > requirements.txt

  Install everything from that file (e.g. after cloning a project):
    pip install -r requirements.txt

Always activate your virtual environment before running pip install so packages go into the project venv, not your system Python.

Commonly used packages for beginners:
  flask        — web applications
  requests     — HTTP calls
  numpy        — numerical computing
  pandas       — data analysis
  matplotlib   — data visualisation
  scikit-learn — machine learning
records.fun_fact: PyPI (Python Package Index) at pypi.org hosts over 500,000 packages — there is almost certainly a pip package for whatever you need.
common_mistakes: Running pip install without activating the venv first
Forgetting to run pip freeze after installing packages
Not including requirements.txt in your project repository

records.title: requirements.txt — Package List File

quick_facts.label: What it is
quick_facts.value: A text file listing all packages your project needs

quick_facts.label: Why use it
quick_facts.value: So anyone can recreate your exact environment

records.definition: **requirements.txt** is a plain text file that lists all the Python packages your project needs, so others can install the exact same versions.
records.explanation:
A typical requirements.txt looks like:

  flask==3.0.0
  requests==2.31.0
  numpy==1.26.0
  pandas==2.1.0

How to use it:

  1. Install your packages normally:
       pip install flask requests numpy

  2. Save what you have installed:
       pip freeze > requirements.txt

  3. Share your project (e.g. upload to GitHub).

  4. Someone else clones your project and runs:
       python -m venv venv
       venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
       pip install -r requirements.txt
     → They get the exact same versions you used.
